horizon.elevation.title: Terrain horizon elevation
horizon.elevation.definition: For each azimuth and observer height: the largest elevation angle, above the plane perpendicular to the radial direction at the site, of the straight line from the observer to any terrain point along the great circle of that azimuth, out to the search radius. Negative when the terrain horizon lies below the horizontal.
horizon.elevation.algorithm: Great-circle rays on a sphere. Exact triangle observer - terrain point - centre of the Moon, tan(e) = (r_t cos g - r_o) / (r_t sin g), evaluated in a cancellation-free form; curvature is contained in the formula. Each ray is covered by a lattice of points half a pixel apart. Near the site every lattice point is evaluated on the finest data. Farther out the lattice is grouped into cells; a cell is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it can reach the horizon already found, otherwise it is walked point by point on the finest data. Crossings of the ray with the lines through pixel centres (the creases of the bilinear surface) are evaluated as well, and the leading points are refined by nested sampling. All observer heights share the same terrain evaluations.
horizon.elevation.frame: local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere

horizon.obstacles.title: Obstacles of the horizon profile
horizon.obstacles.definition: An obstacle is a run of neighbouring azimuths whose horizon is set by the same piece of terrain. obstacle_id gives, per observer height and azimuth, the index of the obstacle in the obstacles list (-1 where the horizon has no data). Each obstacle lists its azimuth range, the range of distances of its limiting points, and its peak: the azimuth at which its horizon elevation is largest, with the distance, coordinates and height of the limiting point there.
horizon.obstacles.algorithm: Two neighbouring azimuths belong to the same obstacle if the distances of their limiting points differ by no more than 10% of the smaller one or by no more than 50 m. The profile is treated as periodic. near_field marks a peak closer than 1000 m.

timeline.windows.title: Visibility windows
timeline.windows.definition: Intervals during which the stated condition holds. '*_visible' uses the scenario threshold; '*_any_part_visible' and '*_full_disc_visible' bracket the partial phase: between them the disc is partly hidden and 'visible_fraction' says how much. timeline.windows.algorithm: Built from the refined event times; 'sun_and_earth_visible' is the intersection of the two '*_visible' sets. Eclipse contacts: the separation of the Sun and the Earth seen from the site equals the sum (partial) or the difference (total) of their angular radii; Earth as an opaque disc of its equatorial radius without atmosphere; located by bisection like the events. A window that touches the start or the end of the computed range is marked clipped.

dem_height_error_model.source: Data stream, 14 November 2026: data/checkpoints/near_field_report.json (20 m product minus 5 m site rasters, 0.64 to 1.1 million points per site, by slope class) and data/checkpoints/height_error_report.json; RMS maps *_toterr of the 5 m site rasters of Barker et al. (2021), read through lsn_data sample_quality. The RMS maps are the producers' model estimate, not a test against independent data. Every product is built from LOLA returns: errors common to all LOLA products are not covered.

horizon_error.assumption: The terrain point that sets the horizon in each azimuth may be higher or lower than the elevation model says by the stated height; seen from the site that is atan(height error / distance), so near terrain gets a wide band and far terrain a narrow one. The same sign is assumed at every azimuth. The height is taken from the stated model: Two sigma for the LOLA products: on the 5 m site rasters twice the producers' RMS error map at the pixel (1 m where the map is empty); on every other product 5 m up to 30 degrees of slope and 7 m above. 'Certain' holds even with the horizon that much higher than computed; 'possible' needs it that much lower. Other error sources (ephemeris, landing position, observer height) are not in this band.

landing_ellipse.assumption: The landing point may be anywhere inside the stated ellipse on the reference sphere. The sample points fill the ellipse evenly in area (sunflower pattern, the centre first). Every point has its own terrain horizon and its own local vertical. The share of points is a survey of the ellipse, not a probability, and it is not combined with the horizon error.

calendar.definition: A lunar day begins when the Sun crosses the 180 degree meridian of the body-fixed frame (the middle of the far side, close to new Moon). The periods do not depend on the site. The first and the last period are cut by the ends of the computed range.

terrain.notice: For drawing only. Visibility, events and windows come from the timeline of this package, which was computed on the finest elevation data; never derive them from this surface.
terrain.frame: Local East/North/Up of the site (site.enu), origin at the ground point of the site (site.position_km), metres. Element [i][j] of up_m is the surface point with north = north_min_m + i * spacing_m and east = east_min_m + j * spacing_m. The curvature of the sphere is in the values. A direction with azimuth A and elevation E points to (sin A cos E, cos A cos E, sin E); an observer at height m stands at (0, 0, m).
